speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in view of the widespread and costly damage to agricultural crops and private property at Westham Island and East Delta, British Columbia, which has occurred in the past 48 hours due to a series of breaches to the Delta dykes, due to high winds and tides more than two feet above normal, and whereas the federal Government has consistently failed to meet its obligations to upgrade these dykes, in spite of repeated warnings of flood danger, 1 move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson):
That the federal Government now recognize the seriously deteriorated state of certain dykes in Delta, British Columbia, by undertaking to meet its obligations to help the farmers in that particular area.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION OF MANAGEMENT AND EARLY RETIREMENT ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Air Canada is apparently so overstaffed in its executive suites that it is making sweetheart, voluntary separation arrangements with 500 of its management personnel at a cost to the company of at least $21 million, together with untold costs to its presently unfunded pension plan. At the same time those people in the machinists' union who do aircraft maintenance and repair are being laid off and dumped on the unemployment lines. 1 therefore move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid):
That this House direct the Government to appoint immediately a special committee of this House, First, to examine the management of Air Canada to find out why Air Canada has 500 surplus management people in the first place, second, to determine the extent to which the sweetheart deals with its boardroom
types affect the quality of Air Canada pensions and the company's profitability and, third, to determine why Air Canada is not prepared to make realistic early retirement arrangements for all its work force, particularly its machinists.

Madam Speaker, today's press tells us that the Prime Minister, dissatisfied with the treatment that he has been receiving at the hands of the private sector network, CTV, has cancelled his annual one-hour interview, by Mr. Bruce Phillips, that has become a regular feature of Christmas seasonal television over the past 14 years. In an effort, presumably, to ensure a more favourable, even if less objective, reception, the Right Hon. Prime Minister has instead arranged for a half-hour session on the publicly-owned CBC network.
It has been a hard year for the Prime Minister and the Members of his Party. We here all understand that, and we have no desire to embarrass him unnecessarily in public. Therefore 1 move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis):
That in the event that the scheduled CBC interview does not work out to the Prime Minister's satisfaction, he should be encouraged to repeat the experiment, for a quarter-hour period, the interview being conducted by either Senator Davey or Mr. Jim Coutts.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETING OF FINANCE MINISTERS-SIZE OF GOVERNMENT DEFICIT
FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETING OF FINANCE MINISTERS-SIZE OF GOVERNMENT DEFICIT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. At their meeting yesterday the Finance Ministers spent some considerable time, I understand, discussing the question of increased spending with a view to creating jobs. I want to ask the Minister of Finance what size of an increase in the deficit the Government is contemplating, and will this increase in the size of the deficit be handled by the federal Government, the provincial Governments, or will it be combined? What is the Minister doing to cut waste in spending, such as the 50 per cent increase in government travel, as well as the 17.1 per cent increase in the administrative costs of Government that I have referred to on a number of occasions in the past?
I ask these questions because it is important that Canadians have some understanding of how big the deficit is going to be, and that it is done in a way that reduces the amount of waste that is present in government spending today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETING OF FINANCE MINISTERS-SIZE OF GOVERNMENT DEFICIT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we indeed had a very constructive and positive meeting yesterday of Finance Ministers. The Finance Ministers agreed that their respective Governments should all pull in the same direction to ensure recovery in 1983 and try to reduce the level of unemployment that we have at the present time. All of us agreed that in the preparation of our respective budgets we would look at ways of improving the economic environment. There have been press reports in that regard.
My friend referred to some of the indications which came out of that meeting. I can tell my hon. friend that we did not discuss the scale of any particular deficit, or increase or decrease in the deficit. We had a general discussion in that regard. There will be further consultations between Ministers. If the Hon. Member is patient, at the time of the budget he will see the size of the deficit planned for 1983. At the present time I am not in a position to indicate to him whether the deficit will increase, decrease, or remain the same.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETING OF FINANCE MINISTERS-SIZE OF GOVERNMENT DEFICIT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, again the Minister of Finance neglected to address my question of government waste and the ability of the Government to cut down on spending.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday there seemed to be some discussion of increased spending on public works and transportation. Obviously the purpose of the increased spending is to create jobs. How does the Minister reconcile this objective with the Income Tax Act and the regulations before us today, which will reduce the capital cost allowance and introduce nine separate disincentives for small-businessmen to increase their spending and thereby increase jobs? Is it the intent of the Government to take that job creation capacity away from small business and
centralize it in Governments where bureaucrats can control the whole process in the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my hon. friend should not be surprised if it is not possible within the limits of the Question Period to answer the three or four questions he decides to ask at the same time under the pretext of asking one question. Therefore I will go back to some of the points he raised. The first one was control of expenditures. The Government has established very strict control on expenditures over the years. In fact, as my hon. friend knows, the Government has appointed a Comptroller-General. That followed on recommendations from the Auditor General and from the Lambert Commission a few years ago. He is an outstanding person who came from the private sector. He has helped very considerably in ensuring that all Departments are exercising very strict control over their expenditures. The President of the Treasury Board has indicated he is reviewing all government expenditures in all Departments to ensure that they are being put to the best possible use.
As far as the question relating to the Income Tax Act is concerned, I remind my hon. friend that the measures put forward in the Income Tax amendments include many provisions which would be of significant benefit to small business in this country, particularly the increase in income eligible for the low level of income tax rate from $150,00 to $200,000, and the global deduction increase from $750,000 to $1 million, as a whole, in terms of the low tax rate from which the small business people are going to benefit.
This is only one amongst many measures included in that Bill which are benefiting the small business sector. I hope my hon. friend will recognize that and support this Bill so it can get passed soon in order that small business can benefit from it.

Madam Speaker, I rise to present the following petitions in the House of Commons to fulfil a Private Member's obligation to give as direct access and direct representation as possible of his constituents to this Parliament. Equally important as to whether 1 personally support the view of petitioners or not, is that through the act of presentation I preserve and extend the ancient privilege of direct presentation of petition to the Crown, through Parliament.
I have the duty, Madam Speaker, to present these petitions from residents of Fraser Valley West who are concerned about proposed legislation, namely, Bill C-10. The nature of the petition is to oppose interference in the affairs of churches or voluntary organizations by Government, particularly any
Petitions
action or legislation that might empower the courts or any governmental body to force churches or voluntary organizations to retain in their employ or membership, those whose moral or ethical activities, characters or lifestyles are contrary to the beliefs held by the said church or organization.
The purpose of the petition is to preserve the concept of the sanctity of the separation of church and state, and therefore asks that Parliament deny approval to, or further proceeding with, Bill C-10 or any future Bill that proposes to interfere in church affairs.

subsubtopic: MRS. MITCHELL-CALL FOR END TO ARMS RACE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to present a petition which was scheduled for two days ago when there were considerable procedural difficulties.
It is my duty to present a petition signed by 430 individuals of the Vancouver East riding. The purpose of the petition is to express strongly that world military expenditures now exceed $500 billion per year and the human race is faced with the choice between halting the arms race and proceeding to disarmament, or facing nuclear annihilation.
The nature of the petition is to call upon Parliament to call for U.N. adoption of suffocation to stop the arms race, including those elements in our minority report on security and disarmament.

speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-132, to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO LIMIT INDEXATION
speechtext:
That Bill C-132, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973, be amended in Clause 1 by striking out lines 14 to 17 at page 1.
He said: Madam Speaker, it is best to begin today by explaining to Members the purpose and intent of the amendment which I have moved. This Party is convinced that the Bill to put a 6 and 5 per cent capping on the Family Allowance is wrong because it is punitive to that segment of Canadian society-children-who are least able to defend themselves. It is our intention as a Party, if forced to it, to vote against the implementation of Bill C-132.
I have moved an amendment to the Bill in the belief that it will make the Bill less punitive than it now is. The intent of the amendment is to remove the capping from the year 1984. It will unfortunately leave in place the capping for 1983, which is unacceptable to our party. Even if this amendment is adopted, we will still vote against the Bill in total. However, it makes the Bill only half as punitive as the Minister wants it to be because it would restore indexing for the year 1984.
All Members of this House, whether they are in the New Democratic Party, the Liberal Party or the Conservative Party of Canada, should be very reluctant in the present economic circumstances to do anything that cuts the income of those Canadians who live at or near the poverty line. We should be especially careful about an intention to cut the incomes of those Canadians two years ahead of time. The present economic circumstances are such that there is absolutely no sense of certitude about the Canadian economy for the year 1984. We have very little certitude about what the economy will be like in 1983, but we are really out to lunch when we begin to think that we know what our economy will be like in 1984. It is not inconceivable that we might have runaway inflation by 1984. It is not inconceivable that the effect of this legislation, if Members do not vote for my amendment, will result in a 5 per cent capping in a 20 per cent inflation world.
Sometimes it is too bad that all Members of the House of Commons cannot attend a committee. If they had been at our Committee, they would have seen that other than the Minister

December 17, 1982
Family Allowances Act, 1973
herself, every outside group of witnesses who appeared advised us clearly not to do this. Perhaps the most compelling and graphic presentation was made by a group who represents low-income citizens in Ottawa.
To put the matter in perspective for all of us on the Committee, they told us the following. In a self-help manner, they have organized a transportation system to take members of this low-income group to grocery stores which have the lowest priced food. They told us that if they were to schedule that transportation for the day before the Family Allowance cheques arrived in the homes, nobody would use it. These are low-income Canadians. Therefore, the day before the Family Allowance cheque arrives, there would be no one to use the transportation system.
They deliberately put that transportation system in place for the day after the Family Allowance cheques arrive. Therefore, their transportation is used. Mothers of this nation who live at or near the poverty line each month take their Family Allowance cheque to the lowest-cost grocery store they can find and buy the maximum amount of nutritious food for their children.
That is the purpose to which the Family Allowance cheque is put. That is the purpose which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) asks us to ignore. In a world riddled with uncertainty and inflation, the Minister of National Health and Welfare of this country asks us to cut the Family Allowance cheques which mothers use to buy food for their children.
When the Minister appeared before the Committee, she told us that the Government must do this, that old age pensioners and families must lead in the fight against inflation. 1 wish the Minister had been in Committee to hear some of the witnesses, in particular the labour union groups who to varying degrees have considerable economic expertise in their research organizations.
The group we heard this morning was speaking to the pension Bill, but they put the Family Allowance payments into perspective for us. They told us that the saving would amount to .05 per cent of the federal budget. That is one-twentieth of 1 per cent. In gross national product terms, that is 1/100 of 1 per cent. For anybody to believe that that kind of expenditure difference will have any impact on inflation is just incredible. In national terms, that amount is so tiny that it will not affect inflation one whit, one iota or one little bit.
The Government's case for the necessity of this Bill is further eroded when the Minister comes before us and says that inflation is reducing, that it is coming down. A number of spokespersons for the Cabinet stand up in this Chamber whenever they have the occasion to tell us that their program is working, that inflation is coming down. Stop and consider that statement for just one minute. It is a true statement; inflation in this country is coming down. However, the second part of the Minister's case is that therefore we need to take money away from families and pensioners. That statement collapses because we have not done it and yet inflation is coming down. We do not need to take money away from pensioners or from children.
Inflation is coming down for another set of reasons. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that on this particular piece of legislation, and the pension Bills which follow, the backbenchers on the other side will collectively begin to meet in the corridors and in their offices and start to exercise some sense of social responsibility. The Liberal backbenchers have an obligation to join with the Opposition in telling the Cabinet they are doing something wrong and we will not tolerate it. They do not have to bring the Government down and cause a general election; they just have to tell the House Leader that they will not stand in this Chamber and vote for this legislation. A quiet word to the Minister and this legislation will not come before us, and on January 1, 1983 those cheques for pensioners and families will go out under the present system, fully indexed.
Our parliamentary tradition, the very basis for the existence of this Chamber, is the belief that in all the ridings in this country people vote freely and democratically for someone to represent them here. Out of the Hon. Members of this Chamber we choose a Cabinet. Cabinet Members come from the Party that has the most seats in the Chamber. But the obligation is on all of us Commoners, regardless of Party; the Government proposes, but it is the backbenchers who dispose. We, the backbenchers of this House, either approve the plans of the Cabinet or make our disapproval known. And it is possible, Mr. Speaker, in the next four days for the backbenchers on the Liberal side of this House to meet quietly, to think through this problem, and to communicate to their House Leader and the Minister their disapproval of these three pieces of legislation which take money out of the pockets of children and senior citizens, which take food out of the bellies of children and the senior citizens of this country.
A growing proportion of Canadians live at or near the poverty line, and when you live there, Mr. Speaker, the little money you get in a world so full of inflation is needed for survival, not luxuries. It is needed for good health, good nutrition, good medical care, good shelter. That is what the money is needed for, and that is what the Minister of National Health and Welfare is asking us to take away from these people.
All of us who represent constituencies in this Chamber know what is happening in our communities. I come from the. community of Calgary, Alberta, and for a number of years now it has had the reputation of being one of the most economically advantageous places to live. I was looking over some newspaper clippings yesterday which reported that welfare rolls in the City of Calgary from October to November went up 11.9 per cent. That is in one month, Mr. Speaker. From October to November unemployment went up from 9.5 per cent to 11.4 per cent. That is almost 2 per cent in 30 days. The vacancy rate in my City in the last 12 months has changed from two-tenths of 1 per cent to the highest in the country, at 8.2 per cent. What that tells us is that the unemployment rate in that community would be somewhere near 20 per cent if all those Canadians who had moved to Calgary had stayed there. But they have not; they have returned in many, many cases to
December 17, 1982

the family home in other parts of the country, and thus have reduced our unemployment rate to 11.4 per cent and increased our vacancy rate to 8.2 per cent.
If that is happening in my community, which has been one of the leading communities in terms of economic growth in this country, then what is happening in the economically disadvantaged parts of this country? We all know about Sudbury. Close to 30 per cent of the people who live in Sudbury, Ontario, are unemployed today with little, if any, prospects of employment tomorrow. What does that tell us about family incomes? Our unemployment statistics told us we used to have one million unemployed and we now have one and a half million unemployed. Statistics show that welfare caseloads are going up at an average rate of 10 per cent a month.
What does all that tell us about family incomes? It tells us that family incomes are falling dramatically. The money which parents have to put food on the table for their children has decreased dramatically, and in the midst of that kind of situation, the Minister of National Health and Welfare stands up in this Chamber and brings forward a piece of legislation which provides that in a time of maximum difficulty, we will cut some more money from those families. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in his last budget decided to take on average $300 more out of the pockets of Canadians who are working.
Consumer spending is cut through those kinds of tactics, and as we cut consumer spending, we notice an increase in unemployment, and then an increase in the number of people who have to go on welfare because their unemployment insurance has run out. These are the people who have taken the consequences of what the labour unions were calling before our Committee "perverse fiscal policy". They used "perverse" in many senses because it is a word which has many meanings, but the clearest cut sense in which they meant it is that it is perverse in the sense of being opposite to what it should be.
With a million and a half unemployed Canadians, what Government needs to be doing today is encouraging Canadians to spend, to buy, to create jobs. Instead we have a Government that, through taxation policy, through the six and five cap on pensioners and families, is cutting down on spending. As they do that, Mr. Speaker, they encourage the creation of more unemployed and it is inevitable that a higher and higher proportion of Canadians will be living at or near the poverty line. There are more in that situation today than there were a month ago, and there will be more a month from now than there are today.
In the midst of all that, the Minister of National Health and Welfare says to the Members of this Chamber: Take some more money away from that growing number of Canadians who are forced to live at or near the poverty line.

The Member will have a chance to stand up and try to refute the testimony. The money is coming out of the pockets of families today. Not only that, it is going to come out of the pockets of families way into the future. It is eroding the base of universality. If the Member says he has read the Bill, surely he recognizes at least that much.
In 1985, when we return to indexing, we will do so on a smaller base. If he has any familiarity with the mathematics of compound interest, he should understand that the eroded base will be taking money out of the pockets of families in this country in ever increasing amounts year after year after year. In ten years' time the amount will be enormous; in 20 years' time it will be horrendous. That is the impact of this legislation, which I gather the backbencher on the other side intends to vote for and will be answerable to his constituents.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO LIMIT INDEXATION

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO LIMIT INDEXATION
speechtext:
You know what would have been better, Mr. Speaker? If Members of this House would read an article in The Financial Post of December 11, they would see it points out with some clarity that there are three major financial elements to the system currently in place to provide support for families. One element is the Family Allowance, another is the Child Tax Credit, and the third is the income tax deduction. For a family with two children and a taxable income of about $26,300, those three elements provide more than $800 for each of those two children. That is taxable income, Mr. Speaker. That means a gross income of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $35,000.
Now, in a just and humane society surely we would think that the poorest people would get at least as much, a little over $800 per child. But under the current system, that is not what happens. The poorest segment of Canadian society, those families who do not even have enough income to pay income tax, get less than $700 per child. Those Canadians with family incomes in the neighbourhood of $35,000 get over $800 per child out of our system, and those with not enough income even to pay tax get less than $700.

December 17, 1982
Family Allowances Act, 1973
If the Government wanted to save money, Mr. Speaker, if it wanted to be just, then we would not have this Bill before us today, because of those three elements of that system which affect family incomes, the fairest one to poor people of this nation is the Family Allowance. The other two elements are not nearly as fair. But we have a perverse Government, supported by what I am beginning to suspect are a perverse group of backbenchers. Of those three programs available for redistribution, savings or whatever, the Government attacks the only one which has justice in it, the only one of those three elements which maximizes benefits to the poor and gradually reduces the benefits as family incomes go up.
What rational explanation can backbenchers on the other side give to their constituents for cutting spending on the most socially just part of those three elements? How can they go back into their ridings and say: "We want to save a little money, but we will continue to give more to the rich or to the better off than we are going to give to the poor"? What sense of perverted Liberal thought is involved in this Government bringing forward this Bill? How can they go back to their ridings and defend this Bill as somehow making a contribution to reducing inflation in this country when it is an insignificant amount of money relative to our gross national product and when it is one-twentieth of 1 per cent of federal expenditures?
Members on this side, in committee and in this Chamber, have continually pointed out to the Government other areas which would have more impact on reducing inflation and would save the Government more money than this legislation. I would like to bring to the House's attention just a couple of them. Last night in committee 1 handed out an analysis which shows that in the year just finishing the hidden interest cost subsidy to Petro-Canada, one Crown corporation, is $514 million. Can 1 repeat that, Mr. Speaker? The hidden subsidy, which does not show up in the Estimates, to one Crown corporation, in one calendar year, is $514 million. There are direct subsidies in the Estimates to that same Crown corporation in excess of $400 million. At that point we are remarkably close to $1 billion, and here we are spending days of House time to approve a measure which will take about $80 million away from families and children. In a couple of days we are going to be asked to approve another measure which takes another $80 million away from pensioners. We do this with the certain knowledge that at the same time we are directly subsidizing one Crown corporation to the tune of $400 million and indirectly for another $514 million. Those amounts are ten to 15 times as great as we are going to save by cutting the Family Allowance in this fashion. Where is the logic in that Mr. Speaker?
When we look at the Minister's Department and at the Auditor General's Report on that department, we do not see massive savings because we are not too sure of what the Auditor General is telling us. However, he does tell us one thing, that in the year just passed the Department overpaid the Canada Pension Plan by $7 million and that the amount is growing yearly.
How did that come about? It happened because they were calculating benefits on gross figures rather than on net contributory figures. It was a simple arithmetical error. As 1 understand it, the Government is going to continue to honour this through the life of those individuals who are first-class senior citizens. Because of a departmental mistake, there was an additional cost of $7 million in the year just passed.
Other parts of the Auditor General's Report show that the Department of National Health and Welfare does not have adequate systems to investigate whether payments to pensioners and families go to those legally entitled to them. We do not know whether there is fraud in the system and, if so, the size of the fraud.
These are the questions which the Auditor General brings to our attention. Before any of us are persuaded that we should take this $60 or $80 million out of the pockets of families, surely we should first of all look into the system that is in place.

speechtext: Why did you vote for the six and five?

I hear the NDP interjecting. That is the Party that in 1979 defeated the budget that was the fairest one for poor people in the decade of the seventies. They threw a Government out of office and now they want to know why we voted for the six and five.
In June, 1982 the NDP was the only Party in this House to vote against cutting their own salaries. They wanted to keep their salaries and that is how they voted. Members of this Party agreed that Members of Parliament should be involved in the war on inflation and should vote for a measure to reduce their incomes. The NDP voted to retain their salaries.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO LIMIT INDEXATION
speechtext: We voted against six and five and for the children.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO LIMIT INDEXATION
speechtext:
The NDP does not seem to realize certain facts, Mr. Speaker. There was a piece of legislation, to be followed by others, which laid down a principle. The only group to be affected immediately by a reduction in income was Members of Parliament and Senators. This Party voted for that so that we could turn things around in the country, but the NDP voted against a reduction in salaries. That is on the record.
As the Bills on six and five came before the House, we committed ourselves to fighting them piece by piece. I would ask the NDP where their amendment on the Family Allowance Bill is. Where were they this morning when there was a vote on a similar amendment on pensions? They were out to lunch, Mr. Speaker. There is a lot of talk but nothing in a legislative sense that makes the world better for anybody.
A Party that defeats a Government that has just brought in a budget that is the fairest for poor people in a decade is guilty of a hypocrisy that will be an albatross around their necks for the rest of their lives. They gave us inflation and they gave us a
December 17, 1982

Government that is attacking pensioners and attacking families.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO LIMIT INDEXATION
speechtext: Are you calling the voters stupid?

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO LIMIT INDEXATION
speechtext:
Every time I see an 8.2 per cent vacancy rate in my city, my blood boils. A high proportion of Canadians are unemployed today and are living near the poverty line because we have a Government that did not understand one sector of our economy. I do not think it understands many sectors but it really messed up the energy sector.
In the month of May we imported 400,000 barrels of oil a day at somewhere near $40 per barrel. That means $16 million per day went out of the country to create jobs in Mexico and Venezuela. At the same time, in western Canada there was that much oil in the ground ready to be pumped at a cost of $25 per barrel. Just the other night 1 heard that in this month of December there are 100,000 barrels of oil per day still shut-in in western Canada. At $40 per barrel, that means $4 million per day is going out of the country. Consumers could have that oil for $2.5 million per day and collectively would save $1.5 million per day. The other $2.5 million would remain in the Canadian economy to create jobs. In 20 days at that rate, we would not need to cut the Family Allowance and in 40 days we would not need to cut the pensions.
Not only did the NDP throw out that budget that was fair to poor people but subsequently it has consistently supported energy policies which have driven the nation into bankruptcy.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Hon. Member knows that that is not a truth. We never supported the National Energy Program. We have said that consistently in the House and have voted that way. The Hon. Member should tell the truth of the House. I agree on the energy subject.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO LIMIT INDEXATION
speechtext:
The Hon. Member agrees with me on the $514 million hidden subsidy given to Petro-Canada? He agrees that it is bad and should go to pensioners? Would he take it away from Petro-Canada? What a remarkable reversal of NDP philosophy! I hope it continues. If any Canadians are living high on the hog, it is those in Crown corporations, including Petro-Canada. They waste more money in a week than would be saved by this Bill.
Last night another Crown corporation, Air Canada, was in the news. The President was quoted as saying, "We are going to rent space or buy it for $30 million. We do not want the $20 million space." He said: "The difference is that we are going into a Buick instead of a Pinto".
That is the attitude of Crown corporations, Mr. Speaker. At a time of economic difficulty when a Crown Corporation is laying off 1,200 employees, it is going to buy a Buick for space instead of a Pinto. The Crown corporations are not controlled by this Chamber; they report to Cabinet Ministers and the NDP put those Ministers in place. Point of Order-Mr. Hnatyshyn

Mr. Speaker, I would make a further comment or observation for your edification or for that of the Parliamentary Secretary. For many years, a number of us in this Chamber have felt that the practice of acceptance of first reading and referral of subject matter, which, in essence, is the content of the Bill, at first reading prior to its being dealt with in principle at second reading, was the most useful course of action for this Chamber to take.
December 17, 1982

In every instance that I can recall going back 17 or 18 years, I say with some modesty that Government always extended Opposition Members the courtesy of informing them of the content. There has never been any aberration from the application of that principle. We have debated the subject matter from time to time, but what the Government is attempting to do here is simply to make available to select Hon. Members of this chamber the content of the Bill. There is no objection to dealing with the Bill but, rather, there is an objection to the process.
This practice has always been carried out in the past by Ministers of Transport, Ministers of Justice, Ministers of External Affairs, Ministers of National Defence, Ministers of Energy, Mines and Resources and Ministers of Fisheries and Oceans. I am not exaggerating. The staff of the Parliamentary Secretary can verify the fact that over the last 25 years there has not been an aberration. It is not a common practice but the practice has been there, and perhaps we should pay a little bit more attention to it.
Let there be no misunderstanding about the fact that the subject matter, the content, was wide open and public. There was no attempt to hide it or impose intervention by way of exception in any way. It was always wide open. It was a recognition on the part of Government that it was not infallible and that, in fact, good concepts could be bettered if they were widely broadcast to a legitimately interested community. In the discussion which would take place in detail on the subject matter, amendments which could be construed as substantive could be proposed, and then the matter would go before the House for second reading debate. However, it should not be narrowly restricted to one or two Members, or even to 102. There are other Members of this Chamber whom 1 am sure have not seen this matter, and if they had the benefit of the half or three-quarter of an hour before the House adjourns for the day, I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary could in fact achieve what it is that he seems to want to achieve. But do not make the mistake that this Chamber will now accept, or ever has in the past accepted blindly such a proposition. It is the principle that we are talking about, not the end. The implication left by that holier-than-thou friend of mine from that little mountain-Hamilton, or wherever it is-that the only people in this country concerned about the subject matter or content of the Bill under question are those to my left is a crock of nonsense.
If the Parliamentary Secretary can in fact get himself geared up to go outside, I think he will find that there are about 4,000 to about 6,000 copies of the Bill printed and awaiting distribution. It awaits some significant action on his part. I trust he is enjoying signing his letters, because I am making two very serious points.
This is a common practice. Do not try to obfuscate it by the fog that you are trying to put over the top of it. We have always been open about these matters. Why not proceed in that manner today? There is nothing wrong with first reading
Point of Order-Mr. Hnatyshyn
and reference of the subject matter to committee before second reading and acceptance in principle. Just simply let us take a look at it. It is the easiest thing in the world to do. That is the process, in any event.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to speak in favour of this amendment, although certainly against the Bill. It is a very short Bill with one clause and two sub-clauses, and only one sub-clause is involved in the amendment. But to address this, I think we have to look at the nature of the child support programs at the federal level. There are three direct support programs, and I suggest we consider them from the point of view of three principles. One is universality; another is the progressive or regressive nature as to whom the money goes to; the third is recognition of the role of parenting given by the different programs.
First of all let us consider the Family Allowance. This is the only universal program of the three child support programs at the federal level. It is one in which payment normally goes to the mother, in other words, to the prime parent, the person who is doing most of the work in raising children. That is very important. That is one of the reasons that women's organizations across the country have supported the Family Allowance, and indeed want it to be expanded, never mind being cut back. Since it is taxable, it is a progressive measure. It goes out univerally, but there is a means of taxing it back from better off families. Indeed, that could be improved if we were concerned about measures of economy, but certainly we can respect the principle of universality and taxing back at the same time with this very important program.
The next one is the Child Tax Credit, Mr. Speaker. Supposedly it goes to the worst off families, although the cut-off point goes up to $26,000 odd for the full-tax credit. It is a selective program and therefore does not have many of the benefits the universal programs do. It is also normally paid to the mother of the child, the prime parent, and for that reason it is a just and good program and something my Party would like to see expanded further.
Then there is the third program, and this is the one the Minister does not like to talk about. When she is pressed on it in committee, she still does not like to talk about it. That is, Mr. Speaker, the child tax deduction. This is not a universal program, it does not benefit everyone, and in fact it benefits most the richest families in the country. There is a lesser

December 17, 1982
Family Allowances Act, 1973
benefit to the middle-income families, and it does not benefit at all the poor families because they are not paying any income tax whatsoever. So it is a regressive program, and one which is continuing absolutely untouched by the reforms and "deforms" which have been brought before us by the Government. Another feature of the child tax deduction program is that it is paid largely to the parent who does not do most of the work of looking after the child. It is paid to the parent who claims the Family Allowance who, in most two-parent families, is the person who makes the higher income. In other words, it goes mainly to the father of the family, and he is making a higher income because his wife is at home looking after the child. It is a very unjust program which gives the benefit to the person who needs it least and who deserves it least by virtue of the fact that he or she do not have the prime parenting role. One might want to dispute how those roles ought to be shared, but the fact is that it is the mothers who do the prime parenting, whether full time in the family or in the work force.
In Bill C-132 and the amendment that is before the House, we have a change in an economy measure brought in by the Government which is going to attack the progressive and universal Family Allowance Program which benefits the prime parent most. It attacks the best program in a number of respects and leaves untouched the worst program of the three.
Why is that, Mr. Speaker? Mobilization has been given as the reason that the Minister and the Government have brought this measure forward. But mobilization for what, Mr. Speaker? My colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) asked this question in Committee but he did not get much of an answer.
What do we want mothers on Family Allowances actually to do? The Minister has not answered that question. The Hon. Member for Spadina suggests, with some reason, that what we are talking about is immobilization, rather than mobilization. This is a measure to frustrate people. Mothers are going to receive a smaller Family Allowance cheque and they are going to feel guilty about it. This is a psychological program that is supposed to upset them. It is supposed to stir them up-to do what? Nothing positive, according to the Minister. I think we have to assume that it is supposed to make them sit back and worry, feel unhappy and be a little more docile so that the Government can do what it wants with its programs.
I did try to explore with the Minister the savings that might result from this program. It is part of six and five, and we are supposed to be putting more money into job creation. We are supposed to be concerned about the deficit and all these other high principles.
When the Minister first explained the Bill, she let it out that the savings would be in the order of $70 million in the two years, 1983-84. Her computation did not include a very important factor, however, and that is the taxing back of the Family Allowance. If that is cut back, then not very much money will be returned through income tax. We dispute what the exact measures are that account for that. The Government
admits that the real savings of the program outlined in Bill C-132 are only $15 million for two years. According to our computations they are only $10 million for two years. Either way, Mr. Speaker, it is a very significant figure. If they want to argue the case on the basis of necessity and having the money available to do other things, this is a trivial amount. Surely we could find ways of getting the money that would be less harmful to the people of the country than this.
In the Minister's speeches she has expressed the pious hope that the matter could be dealt with in graph form so that we could see more clearly the implications of the program. She brought a graph to one committee meeting and I have a copy in front of me. It is very revealing. Some Liberal backbenchers stumbled around and talked about the distortion in the graph. The problem is that there is a serious distortion in the system through which we hand out benefits.
You will see, Mr. Speaker, that the curve goes up. Lower income families start at this end and higher income families at this end, and the total benefits are the top line. The line goes up so that the total benefits are highest for families at the $30,000 per year level, then they begin to go down. It is only around $35,000 per year that we find the benefits reduced to the level that a poor family receives something from public money funnelled through the federal Government. The benefits are lower at $10,000 per year and under than they are for families in the $10,000 to $30,000 range. That is shocking, Mr. Speaker.
One of the reasons for this is that the child tax deduction program is so highly regressive. It only benefits families with enough income to pay income tax and benefits most those families paying a high rate of tax. The Minister is aware of this because it was discussed in committee. It is a well known fact. When she was pressed on the matter, she answered, "It is not my Department. We are not concerned with tax reform. Equity is not at issue here." She completely removed herself from responsibility by saying it belonged to another Department. Mr. Speaker, she has colleagues in Cabinet, such as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). Surely that is what Cabinet is for. There are three programs, each coming under a different ministry. Surely Cabinet Ministers are paid well enough so that they will do the job properly. They should consult with each other and bring in legislation which is consistent and which makes sense.
Instead of that, we are faced with extremely unfair measures, one of which is an attack on the universal system and leaves untouched the most regressive and selective system, the child tax deduction.
I want to make some partisan remarks about the role of the Conservatives in this, Mr. Speaker. It is very nice to see them supporting us on a Family Allowance measure, but we have to recognize that they are rather late converts to the cause. Family Allowances were introduced in the 1940s by the Liberals. They had been a CCF measure and had been advocated by this Party and its predecessor Party for many years. At that time the Conservatives fought against Family

Allowances, but they were introduced because our predecessor Party had advocated them. The Liberals came to the conclusion it was a good program to swipe from us. When they brought it in, we supported it.
The Conservatives had interesting arguments to oppose Family Allowances. The Minister gave a very spirited response to the accusations of the Conservative spokesperson that this was an attack on poor families. I suggest that her very strong defence that it is not an attack on poor families, but is more selective, and is an attack on richer families with greater protection for the poorer ones, hangs her on another point that she has tried to avoid and that is, the question of universality.
She is right in her claim that there has been an increase in the Child Tax Credit, the selective program to make up for the reduction in the Family Allowance. The Minister emphasized the increase in the selective measure to offset the universal program. 1 think she has to admit that the real problem with the Bill is that it is an attack on universality. This is an important social program, a universal one, that gives recognition to mothers of families. The Government is attacking this program. It is not the first time the Government has attacked this program. Limits have been placed on it before. In fact, Family Allowance would be up to $40 per month per child if indexing had been continuous since it was introduced. We have had attacks before; we are very skeptical and we are very concerned about this one. It is not a measure which will save a lot of money this year because of the increase in the Child Tax Credit. It will ruin the base. It is the thin edge of the wedge for attacking universal programs, and it is a very backward step for that reason.

To say, "We have brought this Bill forward; it seems like a small amount, so we should not really consider it, we should pass it through quickly because these people will be doing their part to help in the fight against inflation", is just not so. It is also a psychological

factor. It takes away from the income of people who cannot afford it, people who expect a cheque every month to assist them with family income.

These examples show how difficult it is for families to plan their budgets. Statistics Canada figures show that there are some 900,000 Canadian children living in poverty. A family must earn over $34,000 before the total benefits begin to diminish.

We find that a large amount of the benefits which is supposed to go to the poor families does not, in fact, go to them.
This raises a question which many Members of Parliament have been asking themselves for some time. When programs are established for the purpose of assisting those in the greatest need, why do we find that a great amount of the money being set aside for those families does not reach them but goes to families who do not really need that tax credit? I have held the opinion for some time that we should reconsider whether those families earning over $34,000 a year should receive those funds and whether that money which is going to those families earning over that amount should be given to those earning under $10,000. 1 can name many families in my constituency who are earning less than $10,000 a year and could benefit from that extra amount of money.
Family Allowance was initially introduced for two reasons. One was to help families, mothers in particular, raise their children and provide a source of separate income to the mother, particularly in poorer families, where perhaps the husband did not spend enough on the care of the children. The mother always had a certain amount of money which she could set aside through the Family Allowance to provide the basic physical needs for her family. Those were excellent reasons for setting up the Family Allowance Program. We find now that many hundreds of millions of dollars are going to people who do not need this assistance. This is assistance which should be going to those who live below the poverty line. It is not going to them under the present program. Therefore, all Members of Parliament will have to deal with this question. They must ask themselves, "How will we improve our programs so that those people who are really in need will, in fact, receive the moneys that we set aside and those who are not in need will not receive those moneys?"
There are many things that can be said about this Bill and why we should not deal with it. The Minister states that we need to take money away from children and pensioners in order to solve the inflationary problem and that, in fact, because of the six and five program, inflation is coming down. I will grant the fact that there is a certain psychological advantage to saying that everyone is participating in a program and therefore we are all helping to bring inflation down. We must ask why inflation has been dropping as was stated previously, even though this Bill concerning pensioners and Family Allowances has not yet been passed. Why is that? It is because the economy of this country is in such terrible shape. Businesses are going bankrupt. There are 1.5 million unemployed, and we are not even including Indian people in that figure. Money is not in demand as it once was. Banks are having trouble even lending their money. With all of these situations, the expenditures in this nation for goods have dropped off tremendously. Factories are closing, businesses are laying off people who are superfluous to their needs, and it is no wonder that, with the economy slowing down in the manner it is, inflation is dropping. The amendment to this Bill, of course, is to change what is a two-year Bill to a one-year Bill. In other words, there is a certain degree of inconsistency here which 1 find difficult to understand. First, the Official Opposition voted to support the six and five program. That means that they have in general terms, 1 suspect, appreciated the merits of this program and its purpose, which is to try to reduce inflation so that everyone, not just the needy, but everyone in this country will be better off. Let us get that straight. We have support in some quarters besides our own Government for the six and five program.
Now we get an amendment which proposes that we only do half this program that is supposed to have impact on reducing inflation. We have an amendment which is introduced to say: let us not try to get inflation down to 5 per cent, let us quit at 6 per cent. 1 see the rationale which is that they want to convert what is a super-program based on 6 per cent inflation then being reduced to 5 per cent inflation, to say, OK, let us go to 6 per cent inflation only.
The other thing that really disturbs me is that they say, "When the total package comes in we are going to vote against it anyway". They are sort of flip-flopping back and forth.
We can use figures to prove anything, and one motive of the Opposition appears to be to frighten those people who will be most affected by this legislation. In reading the testimony and listening to debate, one of the things that has impressed me is that it is almost as if the motive of this program were to save money. Questions which one can find in the testimony so far, and in some of the speeches of the Opposition, seem to say, how much does the Government hope to save from the 50,000 pensioners?
In the June Budget, the former Minister of Finance, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), forecast that limited indexation would reduce expenditures on the Old Age Security Program by $105 million by the end of the 1983/84 fiscal year. Now we have every reason to believe that these savings will be much less, because the six and five program is working.
Why is the Government so pleased about these reduced savings? Here is the flaw in the reasoning which we see there, because the objective of the six and five program was not to save money. It was to reduce inflation to 6 per cent by the end of 1984. The less we save because of the limited OAS indexation, the happier the Government will be, because that will mean a lower rate of inflation and, most important, there will be better prospects for pensioners, and for innumerable other Canadians.
Another suggestion on this idea that perhaps the Government is not saving as much money as it had hoped to save, is that the Government will only save about $10 million from the Family Allowances and the Old Age Security Program, because of the six and five program. I hope we save even less than that $10 million because that will indicate that the six and five program has really worked and that pensioners and
Family Allowances Act, 1973
families with children will not have to give up as much as we originally forecast, which is not very much.
Again I remind you that the purpose of the six and five program was not necessarily to save money. I want to emphasize the fact that this is a short-term program. It is a temporary short-term program and it is meant to achieve the longer range goal which is to reduce inflation.
One of the other major problems that I have with the Opposition is the fact that they are twisting these programs to suggest that universality is in doubt. I think that if you have listened to any of the Minister's speeches, if you have read any of the testimony, certainly from the Government side and if you have listened to some of the other speeches, you will recognize that that is not and never has been in question, and that the program of universality is the key to the social programs that are supported by this Government.
This program is meant to reduce inflation; there will be no loss to those people most in need; the Child Tax Credit will be fully indexed and that group of people who are making up to $27,000 a year will not be touched. If the program works as we trust it will, and we do get inflation reduced to 6 per cent and 5 per cent, not only will those people who possibly are going to feel a little pinched because their incomes are suffering, mostly from inflation, but all Canadians will benefit because we will have reduced inflation by 6 per cent and 5 per cent.
I am worried that so much of the propaganda produced by the Opposition is going to have a detrimental effect on this anti-inflation psychology, which one of the Members admitted in his speech earlier appears to be working and which is a state of mind. 1 think that we must continue to enforce that psychology so that all Canadians, those who are in the higher income brackets and those who are needy, will find that inflation will come down. They have lowered their inflationary expectations, and therefore will be better off because of that reduction in inflation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the consideration which has been shown by the Chair, and by the Hon. Member opposite, in approaching this Bill. I will say that 1 recognize there could be some difficulties with this Bill under the references which have been given. Indeed, it does propose an establishment of a board. This board could be seen to replace a board which is now in place and its members could in fact be renumerated at the same level, in spite of the fact there are additional members on that board. That is one argument which I would be prepared to put forward.
I would like the opportunity to explain the real reason for bringing forward this Bill today. At a time when, perhaps, we might have chosen to speak of other things because of the difficulties which are being faced by the Canadian economy, I think this Bill allows an opportunity for taking into account some of the considerations which are in front of the Canadian people now in nuclear energy and matters relating to nuclear energy, and also those facing the nuclear industry.
To explain the Bill, 1 would like to say that much of the substance has been presented before by way of the Bill which the Government presented in 1977, which was called the Nuclear Control and Administration Act. This Bill was not enacted, and it died on the Order Paper. The Bill at that time was designed to bring into focus the development and concerns which have become evident since the first passage of the Atomic Energy Control Act, and that Act was first passed in 1946. There was one amendment in 1974. However, from that period of time we have not had major revision or review of the process to deal with the whole nuclear question in Canada. Since this Act was presented to Parliament, that is, the Atomic Energy Control Act, nuclear-generated electricity has become a very important component of our electrical system, particularly in Ontario where it accounts for approximately one-third of the total electrical power generated. Spectacular advances in the use of nuclear materials in industry and medicine have added significantly to the broad application of nuclear materials throughout Canadian society.
Bill C-218, as presented to the House today, also contains some revisions as suggested by the Canadian Environmental Law Association, and changes by myself and others. The Bill was first re-drafted nearly three years ago, and is a sister Bill of two other private members' Bills, that of the Hon. Member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) and that of the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan). In the context of today's economy, unemployment and serious nuclear industry problems, the Bill needs revision again in co-operation with the interested parties. This Bill includes proposals which would see a nuclear control board created composed of people without vested interests in the nuclear industry. It establishes a radioactive decontamination fund, requires site approval as a first step in the establishment of a nuclear facility, requires disclosure of unclassified documents, and makes the Minister responsible for the board report to Parliament on a regular basis.
The Bill is as complex as the subject, and I readily admit to limitations in being able to fully determine the legal, jurisdictional or other implications of some of the suggested changes.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Hillsborough, the Conservative critic for the environment, and 1 would not support any measures which would threaten the economic viability of the industry, or act as roadblocks for future development. Evidence now available in connection with acid rain, carbon dioxide, and other environmental disruptions, as in coal electrical generation or the James Bay hydro development, suggest that nuclear energy has distinct advantages. No industry, no energy form, no economic activity is without its price in environmental impact. Indeed, the first point I would like to make is that we have really not had the opportunity in Canada since 1946 to consider in a public or parliamentary forum what our nuclear energy future should be, and what relative advantages and disadvantages there really are to the nuclear energy option.
In 1980 the Porter Royal Commission dealt with nuclear energy in Ontario and made a valuable contribution to the understanding of nuclear energy in Canada. Today we really have the worst of all worlds; a mature industry that has produced a very effective high cost technology for Canada's energy needs and is also exportable but is in desperate condition, and a public that has serious concerns and mistrusts, if not in the form of energy, then in the traditional processes which have been involved in dealing with it. I think both the industry and the public are capable of dealing with our nuclear program in a productive way, in the interests of the economy, environment, and our energy future. It is with that hope that I introduce Bill C-218 for the consideration of the House.
I would like to add to my introduction of this Bill an interim plan of action to deal with what is an emergency situation in the Canadian nuclear industry. Over 36,000 Canadian skilled jobs are at stake, in addition to the important energy considerations. Continued energy research and development for future medical, energy, environmental and economic advantages are also at stake, and we cannot afford to dream of future success unless we move swiftly and competently to deal with the problems we are faced with today.
The essential components of this plan of action are, one, the nuclear industry itself must be rationalized to ensure shortterm viability; two, the Government must also similarly rationalize its approach in co-operation with the nuclear industry and the Departments of Energy, Mines and Resources, External Affairs, and Industry, Trade and Commerce and others; three, there must be full Government support and open discussion of our nuclear waste management program; four, domestic reactor facilities must be promoted as part of an over-all Canadian industrial strategy; five, our Canadian energy policy must be directed in both research and development for the use of the nuclear fuel source for our transportation needs and for the heat energy that can readily and cheaply fuel our industries. An example is the proposed Bruce Energy Centre; six, we should develop an effective strategy for the export of nuclear electricity to the United
December 17, 1982

States; seven, Canada is in as good a position as any country to promote adequate international safeguards through an aggressive position with the IAEA. While we continue this important and difficult task we must maintain bilateral safeguards to protect against the abuse of our technology while promoting export sales of the Candu to world markets which have a viable financial status, and as part of an industrial development export strategy in countries where the sale of reactors alone is of questionable value, and where cost considerations are otherwise marginal.
1 hope the Government, while it is occupied with the immediacy of the problems brought forward by the public concerns and with consideration of the nuclear industry's status, can provide the necessary leadership and action. Bill C-218 would allow us a framework to deal with an outdated Canadian statute and, L hope, in the long run serve the needs of both the Canadian public and the nuclear industry.
I ask for concurrence so that at least the subject matter of the Bill can be referred to the appropriate Standing Committee of the House.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to make some remarks regarding the speech by the Hon. Member. I am glad he brought this Bill forward. There are certain aspects of the Bill that I disagree with, and certain aspects of his speech that I disagree with, and 1 am going to go over them in a minute.
The Hon. Member and his party, and 1 and my party, share a concern that-and I will try and put it politely-there is a really scandulous situation happening in Canada. We have criticized the United States for many things, but this situation could never happen there. What I am speaking of is really a cover-up going on in the Canadian nuclear industry, and an unwillingness to debate what is happening. The Conservative Party and the NDP have different views about the nuclear future, but we have in common the desire to have a full and open public inquiry on this issue. It is really a scandal that we in Canada have had nothing but whitewashing of this issue.
The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) stood up at the beginning of this debate and tried to block the Bill because it involved spending public funds. If 1 did not know the Hon. Member, that would add to my suspicion and the suspicion of the others in Canada that Government strategy is one of sweeping the whole nuclear problem under the carpet. We have a vast problem here in Canada with the nuclear industry, Mr. Speaker. We have not faced it as a people or as a Parliament. It has continually been kept out of the mainstream of our political process, but it is boiling around the periphery, if you like.
Let me just give you an example. Speaking in terms that anyone can understand, that is in terms of money, it has been said by some that you can do two things with money: you can either burn it or give it to AECL and they will dispose of it for you. We have spent $825 million for three heavy water plants which the Government wrote off numerous months ago. Its representatives came into the energy committee with this kind of estimate for the write-off. One of the plants has been mothballed and two others are stockpiling heavy water at a
Atomic Energy Control Act, 1980
cost of $! million a year in the hope that a number of Candu's can be sold abroad. But we are not selling Candu's abroad, even though we are prepared to sell them to almost anyone. I am sure if General Zia wanted another Candu reactor today, we would sell it to him in a minute. We are prepared to sell nuclear parts to Argentina, to Korea, or any kind of regime we can in order to get rid of those Candus. We are going to Romania, which is virtually broke. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), on these international trips, is spending about one third of his time trying to sell Candus. It is really quite an incredible situation when you think about it. Maybe that is the right thing to do. I do not think it is, but we should be debating the future of our nuclear industry and the Candu in the House of Commons, not just during the short time we have in private Member's hour.
I will give you another example, Mr. Speaker, of money which has been wasted. There is a $25.7 million loan on AECLs first Candu reactor operating at Rolphton. That has also been forgiven. There was $87.5 million given to the ill-fated Gentilly I reactor in Quebec. It was built on the basis that Hydro-Quebec would purchase the station when it proved safe and reliable. This experimental reactor never did prove its worth, Mr. Speaker, and it has been mothballed.
[Translation\
I do not know how to say it in French, but if it is the same as in English, I would say that it is a lemon.

In other words, it is a lemon and $87.5 million went down the drain. These amounts of $87.5 million, $25.7 million, $825 million are not peanuts, Mr. Speaker. There was another $81.5 million spent on the Douglas Point nuclear reactor, built under a similar agreement with Ontario Hydro. It is expected that we will lose $130 million on the Candu sale to Argentina which we made in 1976.
In a question to the Prime Minister in the House I raised the matter of Canada shipping nuclear rods to Argentina at the height of the Falkland crisis. I wondered what policy we had that would allow us to do that at a time when our ally, the United Kingdom, was at war with Argentina. That was an instructive experience, Mr. Speaker. It indicated that we will do almost anything to save the industry.
Let me suggest that we have to deal with this issue. I am sure that the Member who will speak for the Liberal Party will point out that a Nuclear Industry Review has been published. But Mr. Speaker, that was an in-House review. At the time I described it as an "enigma wrapped in an ambiguity''. It had all the markings of a speech of the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. MacLaren). It does not say anything; it does not deal with the problems.
The New Democratic Party and the Conservative Party demanded an open inquiry. Judging from the letters that the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) and others

December 17, 1982
Atomic Energy Control Act, 1980
have received regarding nuclear matters, the Canadian public is interested in the subject. For the young people of today it is not just a financial issue but, rather, an ethical issue. This whole matter of the nuclear future may be one of the great issues of our generation. It concerns our energy future.
The ethical issue is whether to develop nuclear energy without having a means of disposing of the waste. We cannot deal with the dangerous waste. We have no way of disposing of it properly, yet we are prepared to go ahead with the development of the industry. In my view, that is immoral. It is passing a problem from our generation to a future generation and asking it to take the responsibility or to absorb the result.
It is claimed that the reactors are safe and that there are no problems with them. But people know otherwise, Mr. Speaker, and I point to the Three Mile Island incident. The problem is not that a couple of people might die but that a whole generation could be killed. 1 know that is over stating the case, and I admit that, but I want to point out that there is the issue of the waste of money as well as the ethical issue.
The Hon. Member who introduced the Bill tried to deal with some of these problems in Clauses 28 and 32, the problem of the disposal of nuclear waste still exists.
I have a letter on this subject from the citizens of Massey, Ontario, sent by Isabel Hobbs and David Rietkoetter who write:
We are frustrated and angry because the federal government denied our right to veto A.E.C.L. plans by changing the Canada/Ontario Agreement of 1978, just prior to their arrival here.
They write of a ten-year program for storing nuclear waste in deep-rock storage. Every community is concerned because nobody wants nuclear waste stored in the backyard. You would not want that, Mr. Speaker, no Member would. So we have a nuclear waste storage problem.
Why are we developing nuclear energy if we have waste storage problem? Should we not solve some of these problems before we develop the energy? It seems to me that that question has to be examined, and that we must have an open inquiry on the subject. The Bill does not go far enough in dealing with it.
The Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) spoke about the jobs that are at stake. That is a real problem and there will have to be trade-offs. There are other ways of dealing with the issue of jobs at stake. Perhaps the energy industry could be diverted to other, safer areas such as conservation. Just imagine how many jobs could be provided if every house in Canada were retro-fitted, Mr. Speaker. A lot of energy would be saved and nuclear would not be needed. I know it is easy for me to say that, Mr. Speaker, coming from British Columbia where people do not like nuclear energy. The Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody will probably confirm that the citizens of British Columbia do not want a nuclear industry to be developed.
As the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey pointed out, 30 per cent of the energy produced in Ontario is generated by nuclear means. I do not advocate that we do away ,vith it altogether,
but I advocate that we consider whether the production should be expanded. He also referred to the export of electrical energy. In the publication "The National Energy Program Update 1982" at page 67 the following appears:
It would be prepared to consider some form of support for future nuclear plants, even if-initially, at least-they are built to serve the export market. In the case of a possible Lepreau 2 plant, the Government of Canada is prepared at this time to work with the New Brunswick Power Corporation and to provide immediate financial support to pursue an arrangement with U.S. utilities that would allow Lepreau 2 to be built in the immediate future.
A proposal has been made to build nuclear plants in Canada. We cannot sell the Candu abroad, so it has been suggested that we should keep the industry going, build them in Canada, and export the power to the United States.
When I was in Washington I spoke to some energy officials who thought we would be crazy to do this. They said, "Why would you assume all the risks and probably end up having to subsidize the plants? You would be subsidizing American consumers and what would you get out of it? Perhaps you could keep the industry going in the direction it is going now." I say that is the wrong direction, Mr. Speaker, and there may be other directions that we could take.
Perhaps the Hon. Member who introduced the Bill has received a copy of the letter from the Maritime Energy Coalition in Fredericton over the signature of Mr. Allison Connell written to the Leader of this Party, in which he states:
The Maritime Energy Coalition, representing many people of the Maritime region on matters of energy development and usage, has well-founded reasons to entertain the gravest doubts concerning the safety of the Point Lepreau Nuclear Generating Station.
The letter then goes on to deal with safety problems. 1 do not know all about the issues of the safety of that generating station, Mr. Speaker, but I know that letters come from all over the country expressing concern about the safety of nuclear power and about the disposal of nuclear waste.
I want to add a third point and that is the cost of the subsidy to the nuclear industry. I gave four examples that amount to over $2 billion. I have the figures in front of me. We have spent $2.5 billion on Atomic Energy of Canada Limited since it was formed in 1952. From 1947 to 1979 we spent $3.5 billion on this industry. We have to decide whether it is worthwhile to continue to pour money into the industry or whether there are some other alternatives.
In Clause 28 of the Hon. Member's Bill he tried to deal with the problems of nuclear waste, to which I have already made reference. Also in Clause 32 of his Bill he dealt with the matter of hearings. We want a full inquiry into the nuclear industry; we want an open inquiry. If the industry has nothing to hide, then why is it hiding? Why does it not press the Government for a full inquiry so that we can bring together all these forces? In the end-and I am sure Hon. Members would accept it if they believe in the real power of democracy where issues are debated in the open-we may obtain a nuclear policy.
December 17, 1982

I am looking at the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey and wondering whether he has seen the review of the nuclear industry. It is a real sham. 1 had other words to call it but I cannot remember them; they were much wittier.
The Hon. Member talked about the power of and the role for inspectors in Clause 38 of his Bill. 1 point out that the Government is now doing research on making fuel bundles safe so that they cannot be removed. Even if this worked, it seems to me that we still cannot be sure that an Argentinian or-and I will say it today-a Pakistan or whatever could not take fuel bundles out of Candu reactors and make nuclear bombs.
If another country in the world, perhaps not a stable one, used bundles from Canadian reactors to make nuclear bombs, as I suggested Argentina might do, and it used the bomb, think of the consequences to Canada. We know that even a friendly country like India took our uranium and made a bomb. I love India, but I regret that policy.
Let me conclude by saying to the Hon. Member that his Bill is interesting. The consideration of the subject matter is long overdue. I agree with some of the things he has said; I differ with him on others. But the Member and I agree that these are the real issues: the issue of nuclear waste disposal, the issue of expanding Candu sales, the issue of our nuclear future in Canada at the expense of other alternatives, the issue of the money which we have put into AECL, and the issue of openness. These are vital issues of our generation. They are really important matters about which the public knows, and is demanding an inquiry. The Government stands condemned on this issue. It is really one of the big sleeping issues in Canada today, and the Canadian public must somehow find a resolution. I thank the Hon. Member for bringing in this Bill because it suggests one method. It suggests a small step, but it is one way of forcing the Liberal Government to come forward with an open inquiry into the future of the nuclear industry. If the Government is in favour of nuclear, if it is confident about its policy, if it has reasons for writing off the $325 million, the $87 million, the $25 million, the $81 million and the other $130 million, and if it can justify these expenditures, then what is it afraid of? Let us have an open inquiry. Let us take this Bill and add to it. Let us develop a new nuclear policy for Canada which makes a little sense.
