speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody is one of the more articulate spokespersons on that side of the House, notwithstanding the Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis).
I listened carefully to the assertions of the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kings way (Mr. Waddell). Of course he is always full of challenges and inquiries, whether they be predicated upon one or two letters. I share some of the concerns which he raised. I hope when we return to the House in January that he will have a number of questions to ask before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works when the Minister attends or, indeed, during Question Period. I know he will take advantage of the opportunity provided by the House orders, setting aside Opposition days, to discuss this particular subject matter which is of great urgency to him and his Party. I know and I am confident that he will do that, because he believes it to be such a serious issue.
As in the case of most regulatory processes, the nuclear regulatory process in Canada has developed from a parochial, introspective set of procedures in which a very few persons were involved, to one which provides for public consultation and relies extensively upon the co-operation of federal and provincial agencies having public and occupational health and environmental protection responsibilities. Quite clearly the process is not without its critics, and continued effort will be required to ensure that further improvements are made.
Many of those involved in the Canadian nuclear program like to refer to the country's nuclear safety philosophy as somewhat unique. In reality, there are several unique features such as that of primary reliance upon the ingenuity and competence of operators to ensure a high standard of safety and environmental protection. However, many of the fundamental principles were derived on the basis of world-wide experience. It is the Government's intention to continue to maintain an awareness of new developments and to take these into account, as appropriate, in future regulatory proceedings.
The inter-relationships among health, safety and security; national and international aspects; and occupational, public and environmental protection aspects present a complicated array of overlapping subject areas. The Atomic Energy Control Board has been actively seeking to clarify these. Improved working arrangements have been achieved with the Federal Departments of National Health and Welfare, Environment, Labour, Energy, Mines and Resources and Transport. With the first four Departments mentioned, these arrangements formally recognize respective responsibilities and the current practice of AECB of taking into account the standards set by other departments with regulatory interests.
With the continued application of the AEC Act, a number of improvements in regulations have been undertaken. The following subjects have been identified for this work and several documents have already been produced for public comment, covering physical security; administrative aspects including licence review, revocation, and inspection powers; radiation protection regulations; transport packaging regulations; mining regulations; and rules of procedure.

December 17, 1982
Atomic Energy Control Act, 1980
The joint regulatory process established by the AECB with federal and provincial agencies and departments concerned with health, safety and environmental aspects of the nuclear industry, has proven to be very effective in addressing regulatory requirements. Thus, although all the ambiguities in nuclear regulation may not yet have been eliminated, the major areas of concern have been recognized and are being dealt with on a continuing basis by the single federal agency, the Atomic Energy Control Board.
This Bill before us provides a general statement of the federal role and of the responsibilities of AECB, but in doing so it necessitates detailed discussions between certain federal departments and the AECB on the definition of their respective roles. In particular, it is important to identify those areas where mandates or actions of other federal Departments present real or potential overlaps with the mandate of the Atomic Energy Control Board under the proposed Act. For example, the extensive emphasis on the environment in this Bill, a change from the current focus on people, presents a jurisdictional issue requiring considerable consultation and thought.
In recent years there have been a number of highly visible discussions and debates on aspects of the regulation of the nuclear fuel cycle. These have arisen in Royal commissions, in legislative select committees and in other prominent ways. A common factor has been the questioning of the thoroughness and responsibility for regulatory control, usually with emphasis on occupational health and safety. Questions have included the following: is the regulation sufficiently intense? Could it be improved by change of statutory responsibility? Is the legislation clear, or is it confusing to those being regulated? How much federal involvement should there be?
With a profusion of statements on the situation stemming from a variety of viewpoints in governments, industry and in labour, it is not surprising that misunderstandings occasionally arise. I am concerned that this Bill is a reflection of that type of situation.
The Bill removes a significant degree of discretion from the Government of the day by specifying the Minister of the Environment as the Minister responsible for Part I of the Act, that is, the regulatory section. One must remark that apart from the administrative constraint this imposes on the Government, the choice of portfolio is not obvious. The Bill, after all, covers health, safety and security as well as protection of the environment.
It is noted that a major increase in the number of board members is proposed, more than doubling the present total from five to 13 and expanding the number of full-time members by at least four times and possibly nine times. Without quibbling about the additional cost of such an expansion, I would have to question the rationale for this. While it may be desirable to enlarge the board to cope with new responsibilities, I fail to see why nine, 12 or indeed a baker's dozen would necessarily be an improvement over some other number.
Surely the existing board should be asked to advise on this in light of the tasks to be addressed today and indeed in the future.
In this Bill there are no clauses dealing with renumeration of permanent and temporary employees, nor with continuing employment of existing staff, the status of the board as a separate employer, or the status of employees under Public Service legislation. Surely it would be unreasonable to create a regulatory tribunal which could not keep and pay the pool of expertise which now exists or which would end up in some sort of personnel limbo for want of specific staffing references in its governing legislation.
There is an important new approach introduced here which warrants considerable thought. This Bill would have the effect of transforming the nuclear regulatory body from a strictly technical licensing body, to a populist judge of social and economic parameters having political overtones, for instance the requirement to consider alternatives to a proposal. Surely we do not want to detract in any way from the decisionmaking prerogatives of municipal and provincial Governments, nor do we wish to abrogate the political responsibilities of Parliament. I suggest, with respect, that we need a strong, competent, technical tribunal to sort out the technological imperatives while others, Members of this House included, discharge their responsibilities in the more subjective areas of socio-economic and political affairs.

We have told them very clearly that this is a very difficult situation in view of the fact that there are no sales of Candu reactors in the immediate future. However, there are some prospects in the nuclear industry, particularly for Candu reactor sales, which may prolong the health of those two plants. We said very clearly that the matter would be before Cabinet and various alternatives would be reviewed, and that when a decision is reached they would be the first to be consulted whether there is a shut-down or not or there are, indeed, alternatives. That has been the approach and sensitivity shown by this Government to those plants, unlike that of the NDP which proposes to shut them down. There have been no alternatives coming from them.
At a nuclear facility, where do you draw the line between protection of the workers on the site and protecting the public just beyond the boundary fence? Depending on how you read it, this Bill seems to propose a termination of, or at least a partial withdrawl from, nearly a quarter century of rather remarkable performance by the board in regulation. This fine record has gone hand in hand with the intimately associated protection of the general public and the environment from radiation hazards. Lacking an unequivocal statement of responsibility for workers' health and safety, the board could become no more than a builder of safety walls, unconcerned with what went on behind them. Can you imagine a health authority simply slapping a cautionary quarantine sign on a dwelling's door without ensuring medical attention for the occupants? This remote, outside-in approach, is not in the public interest and does not reflect the experience gained from the regulatory performance to date. That is what I am suggesting the Hon. Member is attempting to do in this particular Bill.
Atomic Energy Control Act, 1980
I am sure Members of this House are concerned that a number of provisions of this Bill fly in the face of the principles established by the Access to Information Act now awaiting proclamation. The conflict is understandable since the Bill was drafted more than two years ago, but it is one more indication that additional consultation is desirable on the appropriateness of certain sections. There is no point in itemizing information access provisions, including, 1 note, a somewhat draconian penalty for board staff obstructionism, when a well thought out law on the subject is already on the books.
In conclusion, I have indicated privately to the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey that I would certainly reflect upon a number of the suggestions which he has made today. I hope there will be other opportunities to discuss this particular subject matter, whether it be in committee or in the House on an Opposition day. I know that the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway will want to rise and speak because it is such an important matter.
In closing, I just want to say that the sudden concern of the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway, who now sits with the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody, for the workers in Glace Bay and Port Hawkesbury appalls me.
